items.stem: A circuit diagram shows a component drawn as a plain rectangle with an arrow across it at an angle. Which component is it?

options.text: a variable resistor, whose resistance is set by hand by moving a slider
an LDR, whose resistance falls when the light shining on it brightens
a thermistor, whose resistance changes when its temperature alters
a diode, which allows a current through it in one direction only

items.why: The standard symbol for a variable resistor is the resistor rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it, showing a resistance that can be adjusted.

items.stem: A student is drawing a circuit diagram to measure the current through a lamp and the potential difference across it. Where should the two meters be drawn?

options.text: the voltmeter in the loop with the lamp, and the ammeter across it
the ammeter in the loop with the lamp and the voltmeter across it
both meters drawn in the loop, one on each side of the lamp
both meters drawn across the lamp, in parallel with each other

items.why: The charge to be counted must pass through the ammeter, so it goes in series; the voltmeter compares the potential at the lamp's two ends, so it goes across it.

items.stem: A closed loop of copper wire contains no cell and no power supply. Why is there no current in it?

options.text: the free electrons in the copper drift round on their own, making a current
a complete copper loop needs no cell, so a current flows round it
there is no source of potential difference to make the charge flow
copper has a resistance far too low for a current to be set up

items.why: The specification is explicit: for charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference.

items.stem: What is meant by the size of the electric current in a wire?

options.text: the total charge that has flowed since the circuit was switched on
the speed at which the individual electrons drift along the wire
the energy that the cell transfers to the wire in each second
the rate of flow of electrical charge past a given point in the wire

items.why: The specification defines the size of the electric current as the rate of flow of electrical charge, that is, the charge passing a point each second.

items.stem: A current of 0.40 A passes through a lamp for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the charge flow.

options.text: 2 C

items.why: Q = I t with the time converted to seconds: 5.0 minutes is 300 s, so Q = 0.40 × 300 = 120 C.

items.stem: In the equation Q = I t, which set of units is correct for the three quantities?

options.text: charge flow in amperes, current in coulombs, and time in seconds
charge flow in coulombs, current in amperes, time in seconds
charge flow in coulombs, current in amperes and time in minutes
charge flow in coulombs, current in coulombs, time in seconds

items.why: Exactly as the specification gives them: charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C; current, I, in amperes, A; time, t, in seconds, s.

items.stem: Two identical lamps are in series with a cell. An ammeter between the cell and the first lamp reads 0.30 A. It is then moved to a position between the two lamps. What does it read now?

options.text: less than 0.30 A, because the first lamp has used up some current
less than 0.30 A, because the meter is now further from the cell
0.30 A, because a current has the same value everywhere in one loop
more than 0.30 A, because it is now nearer the second lamp

items.why: A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop, so moving the ammeter within that loop cannot change its reading.

items.stem: A resistor in a circuit is replaced by one of greater resistance, and the potential difference across it is unchanged. What happens to the current through it?

options.text: it stays the same, because the cell always pushes out the same current
it stays the same, because the pd across the component is unchanged
it stays the same, because the cell alone decides the current
it decreases, because a greater resistance opposes the flow of charge

items.why: The greater the resistance of the component, the smaller the current for a given pd across it, which is I = V ÷ R.

items.stem: A potential difference of 6.0 V across a component produces a current of 0.25 A through it. Calculate the resistance of the component.
items.why: Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I = 6.0 ÷ 0.25 = 24 Ω, with resistance in ohms, Ω.

items.stem: A resistor of resistance 15 Ω has a potential difference of 3.0 V across it. Calculate the current through the resistor.
items.why: Rearranging V = I R gives I = V ÷ R = 3.0 ÷ 15 = 0.20 A, with current in amperes, A.

items.stem: In Required practical activity 3 a student doubles the length of nichrome wire in the circuit while keeping its temperature constant. What happens to the resistance of the wire?

options.text: it halves, because a longer wire gives the charge more room to move in
it is unchanged, since resistance depends only on the metal in use
it doubles, because resistance is proportional to the wire length
it falls to a quarter, because the longer wire gives even more room

items.why: At constant temperature the resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length, so twice the length gives twice the resistance.

items.stem: A second resistor, identical to the first, is connected in parallel with it. What happens to the total resistance of the combination?

options.text: it doubles, because two resistors must resist more than one of them
it stays the same, since both resistors have the same resistance
it doubles, because the length of resistance wire has doubled
it halves, because the charge now has two separate paths to flow along

items.why: A parallel branch gives the charge an extra route, so the combined resistance is smaller than either resistor alone — here exactly half.

items.stem: In Required practical activity 3 a student wants to find the resistance of a length of wire. Which pair of measurements is needed?

options.text: the pd across the wire and the current in it
readings from a voltmeter in the loop and an ammeter
the pd across the wire and the charge that flows in it
the pd across the wire and the length of the wire

items.why: The ammeter gives I and the voltmeter gives V, and the resistance follows from R = V ÷ I.

items.stem: In the resistance practical, why is the voltmeter connected across the test wire rather than in the loop with it?

options.text: because a voltmeter in the loop would read the current in it instead
because it must compare the potentials at the two ends of the wire
because a voltmeter, like the ammeter, belongs in the loop
because pd flows through it, so the voltmeter sits in the loop

items.why: Potential difference is a difference between two points, so the meter must be connected to both ends of the component — across it.

items.stem: Which statement about the resistance of circuit components is correct?

options.text: R is a fixed property of every component, in the way that mass is fixed
R never changes, not even in a thermistor or an LDR
for some components R is constant, in others it changes with current
R only changes in components built to sense their surroundings

items.why: Exactly the distinction the specification draws: the value of R remains constant for some resistors but can change as the current changes in others.

items.stem: The I–V graph for a resistor at constant temperature is a straight line passing through the origin. What does this show?

options.text: the resistance rises steadily as the potential difference is increased
the resistance is equal to the gradient of the line at every point
the current does not depend on the resistor, since the cell fixes it
the current is directly proportional to the pd, so the resistance is constant

items.why: A straight line through the origin is what direct proportionality looks like, and it means R remains constant as the current changes.

items.stem: As the current through a filament lamp increases, what happens to the resistance of the lamp, and why?

options.text: it increases, because the filament becomes hotter
it stays constant, because the lamp is an ohmic conductor
it stays constant, because its I–V graph passes through the origin
it increases, because a bigger current always raises resistance

items.why: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases, and a larger current heats it more.

items.stem: A diode is connected into a circuit the reverse way round. What is the current through it?

options.text: a tiny current, because the diode still leaks a little in reverse
almost zero, because the diode has a very high resistance in reverse
much smaller than the forward current, but still easy to measure
the same size as before, but now flowing the other way round

items.why: The current through a diode flows in one direction only, because the diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.

items.stem: A thermistor is taken out of a beaker of iced water and placed in a beaker of hot water. What happens to its resistance?

options.text: it increases, because heating any conductor raises its resistance
it stays the same, because resistance depends on the material only
it decreases, since a thermistor's resistance falls as it warms
it increases, because the warmer thermistor resists the current more

items.why: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases, which is what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.

items.stem: A thermistor is used in a thermostat that switches a heater on when a room becomes too cold. What happens in the circuit as the room cools?

options.text: the thermistor's resistance falls, letting a larger current switch it on
the thermistor's resistance falls, so the heater stays switched off
the thermistor's resistance is unchanged, but the pd across it rises
the thermistor's resistance rises, and the circuit then switches the heater on

items.why: Resistance falls as temperature rises, so cooling raises it; the switching circuit responds to that rise by turning the heater on.

items.stem: The light shining on an LDR is made brighter. What happens to the resistance of the LDR?

options.text: it decreases as the light on it gets brighter
it increases, as there is more light for it to resist
it stays constant whatever the light level may be
it rises steadily as the light on it grows brighter

items.why: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases, from millions of ohms in the dark to a few hundred in bright light.

items.stem: An LDR is part of a circuit that switches a street lamp on when it gets dark. What happens as darkness falls?

options.text: the LDR's resistance falls, so a bigger current can switch the lamp on
the LDR's resistance rises, and so the circuit switches the lamp on
the LDR's resistance falls, so the lamp is kept switched off
the LDR's resistance does not change, but the pd across it falls

items.why: Less light means a higher LDR resistance, and the switching circuit responds to that change by turning the street lamp on.

items.stem: Which circuit would let a student measure the resistance of a fixed resistor?

options.text: a voltmeter in the loop with an ammeter across the resistor
an ammeter and a voltmeter both in the loop with the resistor
an ammeter in the loop and a voltmeter across the resistor
a voltmeter across the cell with an ammeter across the resistor

items.why: The ammeter gives the current through the component and the voltmeter the pd across it, so R = V ÷ I can be calculated.

items.stem: A student plots I–V graphs for a fixed resistor at constant temperature and for a filament lamp. What do the two shapes tell her?

options.text: the resistor has the greater resistance, because its line is the steeper
both elements are linear, because in each of them the current rises as the pd rises
the lamp is linear with constant R, while the resistor's R falls as the current rises
the resistor is a linear element of constant R, while the lamp is non-linear and its R rises

items.why: A straight line through the origin means constant resistance; the lamp's curve flattens because the filament heats and its resistance rises.

items.stem: In Required practical activity 4 the resistor must be kept at a constant temperature. Why does this matter?

options.text: so that any change of resistance from heating cannot spoil the results
so that the resistor does not become hot enough to be dangerous to touch
so that the cell is not drained by the current passing through the wire
so that the ammeter and voltmeter readings are taken at the same time

items.why: The point of the investigation is the resistor's ohmic behaviour, which appears only if its temperature, and so its resistance, is held steady.

items.stem: A charge flow of 720 C passes through a component in 3.0 minutes. Calculate the current.

options.text: 4 A

items.why: I = Q ÷ t with t in seconds: 3.0 minutes is 180 s, so I = 720 ÷ 180 = 4 A.

items.stem: A current of 0.50 A passes through a 12 Ω resistor. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor.
items.why: V = I R = 0.50 × 12 = 6.0 V, with potential difference in volts, V.

items.stem: Which description matches the I–V graph of a filament lamp?

options.text: a straight line through the origin, in both directions
a straight line whose gradient rises with the pd
a curve that becomes steeper as the pd is increased
an S-shaped curve that flattens as the pd rises

items.why: The lamp's resistance rises as the filament heats, so the graph bends over and becomes less steep in both directions.

items.stem: A 3.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in series. What is the total resistance of the combination?

options.text: it is 2.0 Ω, because the charge now divides between two paths
it is 9.0 Ω, because series resistances add together
it is 6.0 Ω, set by the larger of the two resistors
it is 4.5 Ω, the average of the two resistance values

items.why: Resistors in series are joined end to end, so the charge passes through both and their resistances add: 3.0 Ω + 6.0 Ω = 9.0 Ω, which is larger than either resistor alone.

items.stem: A lamp and a fixed resistor are connected in series with a cell. An ammeter placed between the cell and the lamp reads 0.30 A. A second ammeter is placed between the lamp and the resistor. What does the second ammeter read?

options.text: Less than 0.30 A, because some of the current is used up inside the lamp
0.15 A, because the current from the cell is shared between the two parts
0.30 A, because in series there is the same current through each of the components
0.30 A, but only if the resistor is placed nearer to the cell than the lamp

items.why: For components connected in series there is the same current through each component, so both ammeters read 0.30 A.

items.stem: A 6 V battery is connected in series with two identical lamps. A voltmeter across the first lamp reads 3 V. What does a voltmeter across the second lamp read?

options.text: 3 V, because the supply potential difference is shared between the two lamps
6 V, because each component in series has the full supply potential difference
0 V, because the first lamp has already used up the potential difference
3 V, but only if the second lamp is the one nearer to the negative terminal

items.why: The total potential difference of the power supply is shared between components in series, so the two equal shares are 3 V each.

items.stem: A 4 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are joined in series. What is the total resistance of the pair?

options.text: 2 Ω, found by taking the difference of the two values
5 Ω, the value that lies midway between the two resistors
Under 4 Ω, since joining resistors gives the charge more paths
10 Ω, found by adding the two resistance values together

items.why: R_total = R_1 + R_2, so the total resistance is 4 Ω + 6 Ω = 10 Ω.

items.stem: The specification gives the equation R_total = R_1 + R_2. Which statement does this equation express?

options.text: The total resistance of two components in parallel is the sum of each resistance
The total resistance of two components in series is the sum of each resistance
The total resistance of two components in series is set by the larger resistor alone
The total resistance of two components in series lies midway between the two values

items.why: This is the series rule exactly as the specification states it: the total resistance of two components is the sum of the resistance of each component.

items.stem: A student is writing a key for a circuit table. Which line gives the quantity, its symbol and its unit for resistance as the specification states them?

options.text: Resistance, symbol Ω, measured in units called R, put after the value
Resistance, symbol R, measured in volts, whose unit symbol is V
Resistance, symbol I, measured in ohms, whose unit symbol is Ω
Resistance, symbol R, measured in ohms, for which the unit symbol is Ω

items.why: The specification states: resistance, R, in ohms, Ω.

items.stem: Two lamps of different resistances are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. A voltmeter across the first lamp reads 12 V. What does a voltmeter across the second lamp read?

options.text: 6 V, since the potential difference of the battery is shared between the two branches
Less than 12 V, since the first lamp has taken some potential difference
12 V, since the potential difference across each component in parallel is the same
12 V, but only when both of the lamps have exactly the same resistance

items.why: Both branches are joined between the same two points, so each has the full 12 V across it.

items.stem: In a parallel circuit one branch carries a current of 0.40 A and the other carries 0.25 A. What is the current in the wire leading from the supply?

options.text: 0.65 A, the sum of the currents in the two branches
0.40 A, the same as the current within the larger branch
0.15 A, found from the difference of the branch values
0.325 A, the average of the two branch currents

items.why: The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components.

items.stem: A 20 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor are joined in parallel. Which statement about the total resistance of this pair is correct?

options.text: It is 25 Ω, the two resistance values added together
It is below 5 Ω, the smaller of the two resistances
It is 12.5 Ω, halfway between the two resistance values
It is between 5 Ω and 20 Ω, but closer to the 5 Ω one

items.why: The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.

items.stem: Explain why connecting a second resistor in series with the first increases the total resistance of the circuit.

options.text: The charge now has to pass through both resistors in turn, so the single path opposes it more
The second resistor gives the charge another path to follow, and each path opposes it
The second resistor uses up part of the current before it reaches the first resistor
The supply now has to share its potential difference, so it pushes the charge less hard

items.why: In series the one path is effectively made harder to get through, so the resistances add and the total rises.

items.stem: Explain why connecting a second resistor in parallel with the first decreases the total resistance of the circuit.

options.text: The two resistance values simply add, and the supply is shared between the branches
The total has to lie between the two values, so it falls below the larger
The second resistor adds another path, so more charge can flow for the same supply
Each of the resistors now carries only half the current, so each opposes it less

items.why: An extra route for charge means a larger total current for the same potential difference, which is a smaller total resistance.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes a difference between series circuits and parallel circuits?

options.text: In series the potential difference is the same across each component; in parallel the current is
In series the components share out the current; in parallel they share the potential difference
In series there is one path for charge; in parallel each branch carries equal current
In series the current is the same in each component; in parallel the potential difference is

items.why: This states both rules the specification gives: same current through each series component, same potential difference across each parallel component.

items.stem: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the potential difference across it. How should the two meters be connected?

options.text: Ammeter in parallel with the lamp, voltmeter in series with it
Ammeter in series with the lamp, voltmeter across its ends
Both of the meters in series with the lamp, one on each side
Both of the meters in parallel with the lamp, across its ends

items.why: The ammeter must carry the lamp's current, so it goes in series; the voltmeter must span the lamp's ends, so it goes in parallel.

items.stem: A dc series circuit for testing a component contains a cell, an ammeter, a variable resistor and the component, with a voltmeter across the component. Why is the variable resistor included?

options.text: It keeps the current steady while the potential difference across the component is varied
It makes the current the same in every part of the circuit while the test is carried out
It protects the voltmeter by taking a share of the current passing the meter
It changes the current, so several pairs of readings can be taken for the component under test

items.why: Altering its resistance alters the total resistance of the series loop, and so the current, giving a range of readings.

items.stem: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 3 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor. What is the current in the circuit?

options.text: 1.5 A, from 12 V divided by the total resistance of 8 Ω
4 A, from 12 V divided by the 3 Ω resistor on its own
6 A, from 12 V divided by the 2 Ω difference of the pair
2.4 A, from 12 V divided by the 5 Ω resistor by itself

items.why: The series resistances add to 8 Ω, and 12 V ÷ 8 Ω = 1.5 A, the same current through both resistors.

items.stem: A 9 V supply is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor?

options.text: 9 V, as each component has the whole supply across it
4.5 V, as the supply is shared equally between them
6 V, from the 1.5 A current in the 4 Ω resistor
3 V, an equal share among the three parts

items.why: Total resistance 6 Ω gives a current of 1.5 A, and 1.5 A × 4 Ω = 6 V across the larger resistor.

items.stem: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in series across a 9 V supply. Using the idea of equivalent resistance, what current does the supply deliver?

options.text: 1.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 6 Ω alone
0.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 18 Ω
3 A, using an equivalent resistance of just 3 Ω
4.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of just 2 Ω

items.why: The three series resistances add to an equivalent 18 Ω, and 9 V ÷ 18 Ω = 0.5 A.

items.stem: In a circuit a cell is joined to a resistor, and the resistor is joined to two lamps that are placed side by side between the same pair of junctions. How is this circuit best described?

options.text: It has both kinds of part: the resistor is in series with a parallel pair of lamps
It is a series circuit, because all of the components are joined to one cell
It is a parallel circuit, because the circuit contains more than one branch
It is neither, because a circuit has to be all series or all parallel

items.why: Some circuits include both series and parallel parts, and this is one of them.

items.stem: Three lamps are connected in series with a cell. One lamp is taken out of its holder. What happens to the other two lamps?

options.text: They both stay lit, because each lamp has its own path back to the cell
They both stay lit but shine brighter, as the total resistance falls
They both go out, because the single path round the circuit has been broken
The lamp before the empty holder stays lit, but the lamp after it goes out

items.why: In series there is only one path, so removing any component stops the current everywhere in the loop.

items.stem: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a cell. One of the lamps is taken out of its holder. What happens to the remaining lamp?

options.text: It goes out, since taking one lamp out breaks the circuit
It stays lit as before, since its own branch is still complete
It shines more brightly, since it now receives all of the current
It shines more dimly, since the supply now delivers less current

items.why: The remaining branch still has the full supply potential difference across it, so its current is unchanged.

items.stem: A circuit diagram shows a cell, a closed switch and two lamps drawn side by side between the same two junctions. Which measurement would best check that the built circuit matches the diagram?

options.text: Check that exactly the same current passes through each of the lamps
Check that the two lamp potential differences add up to the supply value
Check that the pair has a larger resistance than either lamp on its own
Check that each lamp has the full supply potential difference on it

items.why: Equal potential difference across each component, equal to the supply, is the test for a parallel connection.
